passage:
The PG in Koramangala had old cupboards, so on his first weekend Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport. He tested the alarm four times. Santosh, his roommate from Nashik, watched from the top bunk.
"Chalo, dosa," Santosh said, lifting his helmet off the hook. Lalit climbed on pillion without one. "It's only two signals away."
On the flyover a bus cut across and Santosh braked hard. Lalit grabbed the seat, heart thudding. At the dosa place he laughed it off, then opened the alarm app to make sure nothing in the room had moved.
Santosh looked at him over the chutney. "Your cupboard is safer than your head, yaar."

qa.q: What did Lalit buy on his first weekend at the PG?
qa.a: Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport.

qa.q: Why do you think Lalit checked the alarm app right after the near miss?
qa.a: Locking the cupboard down completely gave him a feeling of total control, so that small fear kept pulling at him while the bigger road danger got laughed off.

qa.q: What small change would protect Lalit most?
qa.a: Getting a helmet of his own and wearing it on every ride, even for two signals; one padlock is plenty for the cupboard.

qa.q: How does Santosh see Lalit's priorities?
qa.a: Santosh finds them upside down, joking that the cupboard is safer than Lalit's head, and was probably shaken too after braking hard.

grounding: It shows a student fixating on removing a small theft fear while ignoring the far bigger danger of riding without a helmet.

"So? Did you apply for the research assistant post?" Chandrika asked, stirring the rasam.
"No, Amma. I took the library desk job."
"The library? Sachin, Professor Nair himself told you to apply. The lab pays three times more, and it's your own subject."
"Twenty people are applying. What if I don't get it? The library is sure. They said yes the same day."
"And if you do get it?"
"If, Amma. With the library there's no if."
Chandrika put the ladle down. "You'll stamp books all summer when you could be learning from him."
"At least I won't sit at home waiting for an email." He glanced at his phone. "The deadline's tonight anyway."
"Tonight means it's still open," she said, and pushed the laptop toward him.

qa.q: Which job did Sachin take?
qa.a: Sachin took the library desk job.

qa.q: What is Sachin afraid of when he says "With the library there's no if"?
qa.a: He is afraid of applying and being turned down; the sure yes feels comforting even though the lab post pays more and fits his subject.

qa.q: What could Sachin try before the deadline tonight?
qa.a: He could still send the application and keep the library job as a fallback, so he gets a chance at the better option without giving up the sure one.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see Sachin's choice?
qa.a: She sees him settling for stamping books when he could be learning in the lab, and she pushes gently because the chance is still open tonight.

grounding: It shows a student taking a low but certain option over a much better uncertain one, because certainty feels safe.

passage:
I'm Mahima. Last month Sharmila and I took the night bus back to Indore after a college fest. I was obsessed with my phone. I'd heard about phones being stolen on buses, so I zipped it into a pouch, put the pouch in my bag, and slept with the bag strap round my wrist. I woke up every hour to check.
The bus dropped us at the highway stop at one in the morning. The road to our hostel was dark and empty. Sharmila said, "Let's wait for an auto at the dhaba, it's lit." I said no, it's only ten minutes, let's walk.
We made it fine. But I've thought about it since: I guarded a phone all night and then walked two girls down a dark road without a second thought.

qa.q: Where did the bus drop Mahima and Sharmila?
qa.a: The bus dropped them at the highway stop at one in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Mahima wake up every hour on the bus?
qa.a: Mahima was fixated on the phone being stolen and wanted that one risk brought down to nothing, so checking felt necessary.

qa.q: What would a wiser plan for that night have looked like?
qa.a: Keep the phone reasonably safe and actually sleep, then wait for an auto at the lit dhaba as Sharmila suggested, since the dark road was the bigger danger.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have felt walking down the dark road?
qa.a: Sharmila may have felt uneasy and unheard 😟, having suggested waiting somewhere lit and then been overruled.

grounding: It shows a student fixating on eliminating a small fear of theft while ignoring the larger danger of a dark, empty road.

passage:
Warden's note, Boys' Hostel B, Tuesday. Parveen.
Imran (second year) came to the office for the third time this month asking for a stronger lock for his cupboard. He has already fitted two. He keeps no cash at all, in case of pickpockets, and asked whether we could put a camera outside his room. I understand the worry; there was one theft on his floor last year.
But this morning I watched him ride out of the gate on his motorbike without a helmet, as he does every day, overtaking a bus on the main road. When I mentioned it, he laughed. "It's a five-minute ride, ma'am."
What I did next: I didn't lecture. I sat with him and asked him to list what he was most afraid of losing, and which of those a cupboard could protect. He went quiet. I've kept a spare helmet at the gate, and I'll check in with him next week.

qa.q: How many locks has Imran already fitted on his cupboard?
qa.a: He has already fitted two.

qa.q: Why might the cupboard lock feel more urgent to Imran than a helmet?
qa.a: There was a real theft on his floor, so that fear feels close and fixable, while the helmetless ride has become routine and he tells himself it's only five minutes.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the warden's approach, and why might it work?
qa.a: Instead of lecturing, Parveen asked Imran to list what he feared losing and what a cupboard could protect, so he could see the bigger danger for himself.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel watching Imran overtake a bus without a helmet?
qa.a: She is likely alarmed and protective, because the risk she sees on the road is far bigger than the one he keeps asking her to fix.

grounding: A warden notes a student who fixates on removing a small theft risk while ignoring the much bigger danger of riding without a helmet.

passage:
Thursday, hostel room, 11 p.m.
Took the data-entry job at the college office today. Four hours every afternoon, fixed small pay, no interview, no chance of rejection.
Swati thinks I've lost it. The coaching centre near the gate wants chemistry tutors and pays almost three times more for fewer hours, and Ma'am Rao from our department practically told me I'd get it. But there's a demo class, and a panel, and what if they say no? Then I'd have nothing. This way I have something for sure.
Swati said, "Neelam, you'd rather have a sure little than a likely lot." I told her she doesn't understand.
Typing spreadsheets at four today, I kept thinking about the chemistry notes I love making for juniors. It's fine. It's safe. It's fine.

qa.q: What job did Neelam take at the college office?
qa.a: The data-entry job, four hours every afternoon.

qa.q: What does Neelam repeating "It's fine. It's safe. It's fine" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Neelam is trying to quiet a doubt, feeling the comfort of a certain job while sensing the better chance given up 😔

qa.q: What choice could Neelam still make without losing the sure job?
qa.a: Neelam could still ask for the demo class; a no would leave the data-entry job in place, so the fear of ending up with nothing isn't real.

qa.q: Why might Swati see the choice so differently from Neelam?
qa.a: Swati looks at the pay, the hours and Ma'am Rao's confidence, while Neelam mostly feels the fear of rejection, so to Swati it looks like giving up a lot for a little.

grounding: A student takes a low but certain job over a much better one because avoiding any chance of rejection feels safer.

Friday. Vikas got the Delhi internship. His friend Tejas found him a cheap flight from Kolkata. "No planes," Vikas said. "Did you see that crash video? I'm not risking it." He booked the overnight bus instead: thirty hours, two drivers, the highway.
Monday. At 2 a.m., somewhere on the highway, the bus swerved round a truck, and Vikas woke with his face pressed to the window, heart hammering. The drivers shouted at each other. The bus kept going at the same speed.
Wednesday. At the hostel in Delhi, Tejas sent him a road-safety report on long-distance night buses. Vikas read it twice. He had got one fear to zero, and then spent thirty hours inside a bigger one. He booked the train for the trip home.

qa.q: How long was the bus journey?
qa.a: It was thirty hours.

qa.q: Why did Vikas choose the bus over the flight?
qa.a: Vikas felt afraid after the crash video, and cutting out flying completely felt comforting, so the bigger risk of the night highway barely registered.

qa.q: What did Vikas choose for the trip home, and what could guide choices like this?
qa.a: He booked the train; comparing the overall risk of each option, not just the scariest one, would guide choices like this.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Vikas refused the flight?
qa.a: Tejas might have felt frustrated and a little worried, which is why the road-safety report was sent later.

grounding: Shows a student removing one small fear completely while taking on a bigger danger he ignored.

passage: Shreya, you're choosing between the sure seat and the better college that might waitlist you? Let your Tejas nana tell you something. At twenty, I had a letter offering a clerk's post at the post office: sure, steady, low. And a place in an apprenticeship at the railway workshop in Ajmer, where the foreman told me nine in ten apprentices got a good job at the end. Nine in ten! But that one in ten kept me awake. With the post office, nothing could go wrong. I picked the sure thing. Thirty years of stamping letters. My friend Gopal took the apprenticeship, became a senior engineer, built bridges. I don't say the post office was bad, beta. I say I paid a big price to make one small fear disappear. Look at the whole picture, not just the scary slice.

qa.q: What did the foreman say about the apprentices?
qa.a: The foreman said nine in ten apprentices got a good job at the end.

qa.q: Why did young Tejas pick the post office job?
qa.a: Tejas felt anxious about the one-in-ten chance of failing, and the post office felt comforting because nothing could go wrong there.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Nana's story, and what does Nana wish had been weighed?
qa.a: Choosing the sure clerk's post over the apprenticeship; Nana now wishes the whole picture had been weighed, a very likely good outcome, instead of the small scary slice.

qa.q: How did Gopal's life go after taking the apprenticeship?
qa.a: Gopal became a senior engineer and built bridges.

grounding: Shows a young man accepting a low but sure option over a much better, very likely one because removing all doubt felt comforting.

passage: Gurleen had exactly one thousand rupees left for the month, and she spent seven hundred of it on a heavy new padlock for her hostel cupboard. A girl two floors up had lost a watch last year, and Gurleen wanted that risk gone. Completely. Ishita, her roommate, watched her fit it. "Great lock. And the plug point by your bed? It sparked again last night." "It's fine, it just crackles." "It sparked, Gurleen. With your heater on." Gurleen shrugged; the lock felt solid and final, and the wiring felt like somebody else's problem. That night the socket sparked with a loud crack, and the room smelled of burning plastic. Ishita switched off the heater at the wall and ran for the warden, who cut the room's power and had the electrician there by morning. Gurleen sat on the bed, staring at her shiny lock.

qa.q: How much did Gurleen spend on the padlock?
qa.a: She spent seven hundred rupees on it.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen spend so much on a lock while ignoring the sparking socket?
qa.a: Gurleen felt anxious about theft and comforted by making that risk vanish completely, while the socket seemed like somebody else's problem.

qa.q: What did Ishita do when the socket sparked, and what should happen with hazards like this?
qa.a: Ishita switched off the heater and ran for the warden, who cut the power and got an electrician; faults like this should be reported straight away.

qa.q: How did Ishita see the lock and the socket?
qa.a: Ishita saw that the lock guarded against a rare theft while the sparking socket was the real danger in the room.

grounding: Shows a student spending her limited money to get a small risk to zero while ignoring a bigger danger in her room.

passage:
Irawati was in her second year at a Kolkata college, and she had become fierce about food safety. She wouldn't eat from the street puchka stall near the hostel, carried her own steel bottle and wiped her plate twice in the canteen.

Her friend Kiran noticed something else. "You ride your scooty to class without a helmet every day."

"It's a short ride," Irawati said. "The puchka water is the real danger."

"Busy crossings, auto-rickshaws, rain. You've nearly skidded twice."

Irawati's jaw tightened. She felt cross, then a little shaken. She could picture every germ in that water; she couldn't picture the crossing going wrong.

The next morning Kiran saw her at the gate, holding a borrowed helmet and grumbling.

qa.q: Where would Irawati not eat?
qa.a: She wouldn't eat from the street puchka stall near the hostel.

qa.q: Why did Irawati feel cross when Kiran mentioned the helmet?
qa.a: She felt defensive because the germ fear felt vivid and controllable, while the road risk felt distant, so being questioned stung.

qa.q: What would you advise Irawati about her safety habits?
qa.a: Keep the food care if she likes, but give the bigger danger priority by always wearing a helmet.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Irawati's habits?
qa.a: Kiran is worried that Irawati guards against a smaller risk while ignoring a bigger one on the road.

grounding: A student fixates on eliminating one small fear while ignoring a bigger danger.

"Chaitanya, you got the research internship offer from the institute? That's amazing!"

"I'm not taking it, Chinmay."

"What? Why?"

"There's a thirty per cent chance they don't extend it after the first month."

"So seventy per cent it runs the full summer, with real lab work."

"Uncle's firm offered me filing work. Guaranteed. Three months."

"You'll learn nothing there. You hated it last year."

"At least I know how it ends."

"And the institute could get you a recommendation for your master's."

Chaitanya rubbed his face. "I just don't want to be left with nothing in July."

"Then ask the institute what they'd do if it doesn't extend. Don't just pick the sure boring thing."

qa.q: What work did Uncle's firm offer Chaitanya?
qa.a: Filing work, guaranteed for three months.

qa.q: Why does the sure option appeal so strongly to Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels anxious about being left with nothing in July, and the certainty of the filing job feels comforting even though it's far less useful.

qa.q: What small step did Chinmay suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: He suggested asking the institute what happens if it doesn't extend, so Chaitanya can weigh real information instead of just grabbing certainty.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel watching Chaitanya turn down the internship?
qa.a: Chinmay seems frustrated and disappointed, because he can see a much better chance being given up for a little certainty.

grounding: A student prefers a sure but poor option over a much better one with a small risk.

passage:
In my first year of engineering, I was offered a spot on a robotics team that was going to a national contest. The catch was, the college hadn't confirmed whether we'd get travel funds. There was maybe a small chance we wouldn't go at all.

My roommate Lakshmi said, "Even if we don't travel, you'll build a real robot."

But I kept thinking about that small chance of all that work leading nowhere. So I joined the weekend coding club instead, where everything was fixed and nothing could go wrong.

The robotics team went. They placed fourth. The club was fine, but I learnt almost nothing new.

I'm Tanvir, and I still catch myself choosing the thing with no surprises over the thing that's actually better.

qa.q: Where did the robotics team place?
qa.a: The team went and placed fourth.

qa.q: Why did the coding club feel like the better choice to Tanvir at the time?
qa.a: Tanvir felt uneasy about the small chance of not travelling, and the fixed, certain club felt safe and comforting.

qa.q: What could Tanvir try next time a sure-but-small option competes with a better one?
qa.a: Tanvir could list what each option gives even in the worst case, like Lakshmi's point about building a real robot, before deciding.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see Tanvir's choice now?
qa.a: Lakshmi might feel sorry that Tanvir missed out, since Lakshmi saw value in the team even without travel.

grounding: A student chooses a sure but lesser option over a much better one because a small risk feels too uncomfortable.

passage:
Placement cell note, third year. Written by Yogesh, placement officer.
Gurleen came in today to accept an internship at a small local firm: guaranteed, but mostly photocopying, in her own words. She had also been shortlisted for a research internship at the national lab, a far better fit for her, with a good chance of selection after one more interview.
She said, "The local one is a sure thing. If I go for the lab and don't get it, I'll have nothing. I just want zero risk this summer."
I pointed out that she could hold the local offer for a week while she did the lab interview. She hadn't thought of that. The certain option had felt so safe that she hadn't looked at how much better the other was.
What I did next: I emailed the local firm for a one-week extension, which they gave, and booked her a mock interview for Thursday.

qa.q: What did Gurleen say the local internship was mostly?
qa.a: Gurleen said it was mostly photocopying.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen want to accept the local firm right away?
qa.a: Gurleen felt anxious about ending the summer with nothing, so the sure option felt safe even though it was far worse.

qa.q: What did Yogesh suggest, and why was it sensible?
qa.a: Holding the local offer for a week while doing the lab interview, so Gurleen could try for the better option without losing the sure one.

qa.q: How might the local firm see the request for an extension?
qa.a: The firm seems relaxed about it, since they gave the one-week extension.

grounding: Shows, in a placement officer's note, a student about to accept a sure but poor internship over a much better, uncertain one.

passage:
Tuesday night.
I bought a third lock for my hostel cupboard today. Nobody's cupboard has been broken into in two years, but I wanted it to be impossible. Zero chance. It felt so good clicking all three shut.
Then Imran walked back from the library with me at eleven, down the unlit road behind the sports ground, and said, "You know this road is the actual danger, right? Not your cupboard."
I got annoyed. But he's right. I walk that road alone four nights a week because it's shorter. I've never thought about it, because there's no lock for it. You can't make a road zero risk, so I just ignored it.
New plan: I'll take the lit main road, even though it's ten minutes longer, and walk with the library group when they leave at ten. And tomorrow I'll ask the warden why that back road has no lights.
Himani

qa.q: How many locks does Himani's cupboard have now?
qa.a: Himani's cupboard has three locks now.

qa.q: Why did clicking the three locks shut feel so good to Himani?
qa.a: Himani felt safe and relieved making one small risk impossible, which was comforting even though the cupboard was not the real danger.

qa.q: What is Himani's new plan, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Taking the lit main road, walking with the library group and asking the warden about lights, which cuts the bigger risk even if not to zero.

qa.q: How does Imran see Himani's cupboard locks?
qa.a: Imran thinks the cupboard isn't the real danger and points to the unlit road as the thing worth worrying about.

grounding: Shows a student fixed on eliminating one small fear while overlooking a bigger danger, until a friend points it out.

passage:
The Dussehra fair had turned the village ground into a maze of lights, and Tejas, home from college, refused every stall. "Pani puri? No. That water could make me sick. I'm not eating anything here." He even rubbed sanitiser on his hands after touching the ride tickets.
At ten his friends waved him onto the back of a scooter already carrying two people. No helmets, and a dark road full of trucks back to the village.
Ritu, his cousin, caught his arm. "You won't eat one pani puri, but you'll ride triple on the highway?"
"That's different," Tejas snapped. "Everyone rides like that."
"Then everyone's wrong." She nodded at her brother's jeep. "Ride with us."
Tejas glared, cheeks hot, but climbed into the jeep and sat silently all the way home.

qa.q: Where did Ritu ask Tejas to ride?
qa.a: She asked him to ride with them in her brother's jeep.

qa.q: Why did Tejas snap at Ritu?
qa.a: He felt caught out and angry, because his careful food rule made him feel safe and he didn't want to admit the scooter ride was the bigger danger.

qa.q: What would you advise Tejas before the next fair?
qa.a: Compare the risks honestly: relax a little about the food, and never ride triple without a helmet on a dark road.

qa.q: How did Ritu see the scooter ride?
qa.a: Ritu saw it as far more dangerous than any stall food, and she cared enough to stop him and offer a safer way home.

grounding: Shows a student fixating on one small fear while ignoring a much bigger danger.
